**Mastercard joins ECB's cross-currency instant payments pilot on TIPS**

*The card network's participation in a central bank pilot for cross-currency instant settlement on TIPS signals its intent to compete on account-to-account rails, not just card ones.*

Mastercard is working with Danmarks Nationalbank and Sveriges Riksbank on a pilot to enable instant cross-currency payments via the ECB's Target Instant Payment Settlement platform. The pilot connects Danish krone and Swedish krona payments through TIPS, which until now has handled only euro-denominated instant transfers. Mastercard's role involves providing FX settlement capability alongside the instant payment leg.

The significance is less about the pilot's immediate scope and more about what it reveals. A card network embedding itself into central bank instant payment infrastructure marks a strategic shift. Mastercard is positioning to play in account-to-account cross-border flows, not merely defend its card volumes against them. With the Instant Payments Regulation mandating euro instant payment capability across the EU, cross-currency extension is the logical next frontier, and Mastercard is ensuring it has a seat at the table.

For European banks and payment processors, the question is whether the card networks' involvement in these pilots accelerates or complicates the push for domestic payment sovereignty. The same week Visa pledged €500m in European investment, Mastercard is quietly integrating into the plumbing that some policymakers hoped would reduce dependence on the international card schemes.

*Sources: [Mastercard joins Tips cross-currency pilot](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47839/mastercard-joins-tips-cross-currency-pilot) — Finextra | [Mastercard Joins European Cross-Border Instant Payments Pilot](https://www.pymnts.com/news/cross-border-commerce/cross-border-payments/2026/mastercard-joins-european-cross-border-instant-payments-pilot/) — PYMNTS | [Mastercard Pilots Instant Cross-Border Payments and FX Settlement](https://www.paymentsjournal.com/mastercard-pilots-instant-cross-border-payments-and-fx-settlement/amp/) — PaymentsJournal*

**OpenPayd pursues Nasdaq listing via $1.15bn SPAC deal**

*The UK-headquartered embedded finance infrastructure provider is targeting a public listing through a SPAC merger, offering a rare market test of investor appetite for European banking-as-a-service platforms.*

OpenPayd has announced plans to list on Nasdaq through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, in a deal valuing the combined entity at approximately $1.15bn. The transaction includes $276m in new capital. OpenPayd provides embedded accounts, FX, domestic and cross-border payments, open banking connectivity and stablecoin on- and off-ramps to business clients.

The listing is notable for several reasons. European embedded finance providers have largely remained private, funded by venture capital. OpenPayd choosing the SPAC route to a US exchange, rather than a conventional IPO or a London listing, reflects both the difficulty of European fintech IPOs and the continued pull of US capital markets for infrastructure-layer businesses. It also tests whether public market investors see banking-as-a-service as a sustainable business model rather than a venture-stage bet.

For the broader sector, the deal may set a valuation benchmark. If OpenPayd successfully lists, it creates a public comparable for other European embedded finance and payments infrastructure businesses considering exits or fundraising. If it struggles post-listing, it may reinforce caution among investors who have already cooled on fintech multiples since 2022.

*Sources: [OpenPayd to Go Public via $276M SPAC Deal, Targets Nasdaq Listing](https://www.financemagnates.com/fintech/openpayd-to-go-public-via-276m-spac-deal-targets-nasdaq-listing/) — Finance Magnates | [OpenPayd Targets Nasdaq Listing in $1.15 Billion Deal](https://blockster.com/openpayd-targets-nasdaq-listing-in-115-billion-deal) — Blockster*

**NatWest automates invoice finance data collection with Validis**

*NatWest's integration of automated financial data extraction into its invoice finance operations shows how open finance principles are reaching beyond consumer payments into commercial lending workflows.*

NatWest has partnered with Validis, a financial data automation platform, to automate the collection of client financial data within its invoice finance business. The integration replaces manual processes for gathering and verifying the accounting data that underpins lending decisions, reducing turnaround times and the operational burden on both the bank and its SME clients.

Invoice finance has historically been paper-heavy and relationship-driven, with lenders relying on periodic manual submissions of management accounts and aged debtor reports. Automating this via direct connections to clients' accounting systems applies the same logic as open banking, using API-based data sharing to replace manual document exchange, but in a commercial lending context that open banking's retail-focused APIs do not currently reach.

This matters because it illustrates where open finance value is being realised today. While regulatory frameworks such as PSD3 and the EU's open finance proposals are still being finalised, banks are already building automated data pipelines for specific commercial use cases. For fintechs selling into trade finance and working capital, NatWest's move confirms demand from tier-one banks for these capabilities.

*Sources: [NatWest works with Validis to automate financial data collection within invoice finance](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/natwest-works-with-validis-to-automate-financial-data-collection-within-invoice-finance/) — Open Banking Expo*

**Australia's fintechs push data standards body on open finance consistency**

*Industry feedback to Australia's Data Standards Body highlights implementation friction that European open finance frameworks will face as they expand beyond banking data.*

Australian fintechs have told the country's Data Standards Body that clarity and consistency in technical standards are paramount as the Consumer Data Right framework extends from open banking into energy and broader financial services. The feedback, reported by Banking Day, reflects growing frustration with inconsistencies across sectors that share the same underlying data-sharing framework but implement it differently.

Australia's CDR is the most advanced multi-sector open data regime in operation, having launched open banking in 2020, open energy in 2022 and open finance from 2025. The implementation challenges surfacing there are directly relevant to Europe, where the proposed Financial Data Access framework aims to extend data-sharing obligations beyond payment accounts. The Australian experience suggests that technical interoperability across sectors is harder to maintain than establishing it within a single one.

For European product teams planning for open finance, the lesson is practical: standards divergence across data domains creates integration costs that erode the theoretical benefits of a unified framework. Getting the data standards architecture right early is materially cheaper than retrofitting consistency later.

*Sources: [Fintechs tell Data Standards Body 'clarity and consistency are paramount'](https://www.bankingday.com/fintechs-tell-data-standards-body-clarity-and-consistency-are-paramount) — Banking Day*
